To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the risk of asthma in swine-confinement facility workers is higher than in the general population, and that the risk of occupational asthma in swines-confinement facility employees is higher than in non-exposed controls.

1) the majority of swine confinement facility (SCF) workers have respiratory symptoms; 2) the majority of SCF workers have evidence of airway inflammation; 3) the majority of workers have positive specific inhalation challenges (SICs); and 4) there is a significant association between positive SICs and the presence of respiratory symptoms.
the three workers developed symptoms consistent with occupational asthma, and that the three workers were exposed to dusts and/or gases generated in swine confinement facilities.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the main factors affecting the quality of the air inside a swine confinement facility, and their relationship with the health of the workers exposed to this environment.
the development of an effective, non-toxic and environmentally friendly method to remove the organic pollutants from the aqueous solution.
the study of occupational asthma caused by inhalation of swine confinement dust.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no conclusive evidence that there is a causal association between exposure to swine confinement dust and occupational asthma.
the three cases of asthma reported in the article were not caused by the work in a swine confinement facility.
the evidence is insufficient to conclude whether or not there is an association between exposure to swine dust and development of asthma.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have identified three cases of occupational asthma in employees of swine confinement facilities.
the three cases of apparent occupational asthmas were caused by the swine manure dust.

we have found that the prevalence of asthma is high in swine confinement facilities, that there are a number of potential exposures that could be causing asthma, that there are several potential mechanisms of action of these exposures that could be inducing asthma, and that the prevalence of sensitization to dust and dust components is high.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the health of swine confinement employees is not being monitored and that there is no way for them to know whether they are exposed to respiratory hazards at their workplaces.
the risk of occupational asthma is higher than previously thought, and that it is not limited to the health care sector.
there is no one-size-fits-all solution to the problem of occupational asthma.
